label: Rotating sounding rocket (LUCI)
text: Blue Origin's New Shepard sounding rocket can produce lunar gravity for burn tests by spinning (centrifugal acceleration).
quote: Blue Origin New Shepard sounding rocket yields Lunar gravity by using centrifugal acceleration.

label: LUCI hypothesis
text: NASA's LUCI team hypothesised that some materials are more flammable in partial gravity than on Earth, with implications for NASA's 1-g screening test.
quote: Hypothesis: some materials burning in partial-g are more flammable than on Earth. This has important implications for the current 1-g material screening method used by NASA.

label: LUCI
text: LUCI burned a cotton-fiberglass fabric and a 4-mm acrylic (PMMA) rod together in air at normal pressure in simulated lunar gravity.
quote: Two samples are burned simultaneously in air at normal pressure: Cotton-fiberglass composite fabric sheet and a 4-mm diameter rod of acrylic plastic (polymethyl methacrylate).

label: LUCI
text: After launch-provider delays, LUCI finally launched on 4 February 2025.
quote: Initial Planned launch was Spring 2023, Launch provider delay initially delayed launch into late Summer early Fall 2024, until it finally launched Feb 4 2025

label: FM2
text: FM2 will perform burn tests on the lunar surface; as of December 2025 it was planned to launch in late 2026.
quote: performing burn tests on the Lunar surface in the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment which is planned to launch in late 2026

label: FM2
text: FM2 will fly on an uncrewed SpaceX Human Lander System test flight.
quote: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment which will fly on a SpaceX Human Lander System unmanned test flight.

label: 0 g vs lunar g
text: Configurations that cannot support a flame in low gravity could support one at lunar gravity.
quote: Configurations that will not support a flame in low-gravity could support a flame in lunar-gravity

label: Caveat: material-dependent
text: How a material's self-extinguishing oxygen level varies with gravity depends on the material.
quote: Variation of MOC with gravity level is dependent on the material

label: No partial-g acceptance criterion
text: NASA still needs work to establish a partial-gravity flammability acceptance criterion.
quote: Additional work is needed to establish a partial gravity flammability acceptance criterion

label: Tiny lunar data set
text: Because partial-gravity test platforms are scarce, the data set of lunar flammability tests is very small.
quote: Owing to lack of access to partial gravity test platforms, the data set of lunar flammability tests is very small

label: NASA's lunar-g test plan
text: NASA planned to quantify the lunar oxygen-limit shift with models, low-gravity aircraft, a drop-tower centrifuge and a rotating suborbital capsule, anchored by a lunar lander test.
quote: We are developing a plan to quantify the magnitude of ∆%O2 using a combination of modeling, low-gravity aircraft, drop tower centrifuge, and rotating capsule in a sub-orbital flight to be anchored by a lunar lander test

label: Lunar lander (CLPS)
text: A lunar-lander (CLPS) flammability experiment provides 'lunar truth', but its tests are very limited in size and number.
quote: Provides a “Lunar truth” but tests are very limited in size and number

label: Parabolic aircraft
text: Parabolic aircraft give about 20 s of direct partial-gravity burning.
quote: Parabolic Aircraft 20 sec Direct partial-g burn

label: Drop-tower centrifuge
text: A centrifuge rig in NASA Glenn's Zero Gravity Facility drop tower gives 5 s of direct partial-gravity burning to measure flammability limits.
quote: ZGF Centrifuge Rig 5 sec Direct partial-g burn – flammability limits

label: EVA suit
text: US EVA suits used on ISS operate at 4.3 psia with 100% oxygen by volume.
quote: EVA suit: 4.3 psia, 100% O2 by volume (U.S. suits on ISS)

label: Blow-off at 1 g and lunar g
text: At both 1 g and lunar gravity, flame extinction near the limit is by blow-off.
quote: In both 1-g and lunar conditions, extinction is by blow-off

label: Lunar 'goldilocks zone'
text: Lunar gravity widens flammability limits for some materials: a 'goldilocks zone' with less convective heat loss but enough buoyant flow to resupply oxygen.
quote: Lunar gravity has been found to increase the limits of flammability for some materials compared to Earth gravity, presenting a goldilocks zone of reduced convective heat loss, while generating enough buoyant flow to replenish fresh oxygen into the flame zone.

label: HLS and lunar rover atmospheres
text: FM2 can replicate the two atmospheres of immediate interest to NASA's Human Lander System and lunar rover: 21% O2 at 14.7 psia and 34% O2 at 8.2 psia.
quote: specifically 21% oxygen at 14.7 psia, and 34% oxygen at 8.2 psia, which are of immediate interest to the Human Lander System (HLS) and Lunar Rover.

label: FM2
text: FM2 will provide the reference for how materials burn under long-term lunar gravity, to help mitigate fire risk for surface missions.
quote: It will provide the reference for how materials burn under the effect of long term Lunar gravity to help understand and mitigate the risk for future surface exploration missions.

label: Counterexample: Nomex
text: Counterexample: Nomex HT90-40 behaved differently from other materials; gravity strongly affected its flammability.
quote: Gravity has significant effects on the material’s flammability. o Nomex HT90-40® behaves differently than other materials when burned.

label: Earth tests can mislead
text: Materials that are not flammable on Earth can become flammable when oxygen level, cabin pressure or gravity change.
quote: Materials that are not flammable on Earth can become flammable when these conditions change.

label: FM2
text: FM2's planned lunar fire experiments will determine the limiting oxygen concentration of a flight-relevant material (Synergy Pro).
quote: Planned fire experiments on the moon. Currently scheduled in the next few years. Will determine limiting oxygen concentration (LOC) for a flight-relevant material (Synergy Pro).

label: Flammability map
text: The FM2 team's flammability map bounds a flammable region by blow-off extinction and radiative extinction against flow velocity or gravity level.
quote: Flow Velocity (or Gravity Level) Flammable Region Blow-off Extinction Radiative Extinction

label: Factor of safety
text: If confirmed for more materials, NASA may need to add a factor of safety to 1-g flammability limits.
quote: If proven for more materials, this may indicate the need to include a factor of safety on 1g flammability limits.

label: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
text: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 is the main method used to assess flammability of materials for habitable U.S. spacecraft.
quote: NASA STD 6001 Test 1 is the major method used to assess flammability of materials intended for use in habitable environments of U.S. spacecraft.

label: Test 1 is pass/fail
text: Test 1 is a pass/fail upward flame-propagation test run in the most severe oxygen and pressure environment expected in the spacecraft.
quote: The method is a pass/fail upward flame propagation test conducted in the most severe flaming combustion environment (oxygen concentration, pressure) expected in the spacecraft

label: Range of survivable g
text: For Mylar, there appears to be a range of gravity levels within which a flame can survive.
quote: There appears to be a range of g-levels within which a flame can survive.

label: Caveat: sparse data
text: With so few data points, the exact shapes of these flammability curves and their minimums are not known.
quote: Given the sparcity of points, the exact shapes of the curves are not known, nor are the absolute minimums.

label: ISS atmosphere
text: The Space Shuttle and ISS have operated at sea-level conditions: air with 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen at 14.7 psia.
quote: the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have operated at normal sea-level conditions (air, 21% oxygen and 79% nitrogen by volume at 14.7 psia total pressure)

label: ISS pre-breathe
text: Spacecraft materials are tested at ISS's most severe environment: 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia, the pre-breathe atmosphere for spacewalks.
quote: currently 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia which is the pre-breath environment on the ISS for spacewalks

label: Lower pressure, more O2
text: Lowering cabin pressure while holding oxygen partial pressure constant raises oxygen concentration, which increases material flammability.
quote: Keeping oxygen partial pressure constant while reducing total pressure has the effect of increasing the concentration of oxygen which in turn leads to increased flammability of materials.

label: Apollo 1 lesson
text: A major lesson of the Apollo 1 fire: it is impossible to eliminate all ignition sources.
quote: One of the major lessons learned from the Apollo 1 fire is that it is impossible to eliminate all ignition sources

label: Spacecraft ventilation
text: 30 cm/s is a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity.
quote: with a concurrent flow of 30 cm/s, which is a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity

label: Little partial-g data (1999)
text: Very few studies had experimentally treated gravity as a variable for flame spread in purely buoyant flow.
quote: However, very few have considered (especially experimentally) purely-buoyant flow influences, using gravity as a variable.

label: Reduced-gravity aircraft
text: Reduced-gravity aircraft can simulate partial gravity; a special device was developed to improve that simulated environment.
quote: A significant aspect of the experimental effort is to use a special device to improve the simulated partial-gravity environment achievable aboard reduced-gravity aircraft facilities.

label: U-shaped boundary (KC-135 data)
text: Flight data show the downward-spread flammability boundary versus gravity is U-shaped: residence-time extinction at high g, radiative-loss extinction at low g.
quote: The downward spreading boundary is U-shaped showing the dual extinction limits (insufficient residence time in high g, radiative loss in low g) now predicted by several diffusion flame models.

label: Parabolic flight (KC-135)
text: NASA's KC-135 parabolic aircraft provided partial-gravity environments of 0.1, 0.16 and 0.38 g for flame spread tests.
quote: Flight tests were performed onboard the NASA KC-135 aircraft providing partial-gravity environments of 0.1, 0.16, and 0.38 g/gEarth.

label: 1-g screening
text: NASA relies on a 1-g screening test; a material that passes is considered safe for spaceflight.
quote: NASA relies on a 1-g test for screening material flammability for flight. If a material passes this test, then it is considered safe for spaceflight.

label: 1 g may not be the worst case
text: Microgravity research suggests normal gravity may not be the most flammable condition for a material.
quote: However, microgravity research has suggested that normal gravity may not represent the most flammable condition for a material.

label: Burns at 0 g or lunar g, not 1 g
text: Some materials that will not burn at 1 g will burn at 0 g with a low-speed flow, or at partial gravity such as lunar.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

label: Near the most flammable condition
text: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.
quote: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

label: Quenching and blowoff branches
text: NASA's flammability boundary (after T'ien 1986) has a quenching branch and a blowoff branch, plotted against gravity level or characteristic flow speed.
quote: Flammability Boundary Quenching Branch Blowoff Branch % O2 Flame No Flame 1-g Studies Gravity Level (g/gEarth) or Characteristic Flow Speed (cm/s)

label: 34% O2 + lunar g
text: 34% oxygen combined with lunar gravity could be quite challenging for fire safety.
quote: 34% + Lunar-g could be quite challenging from the point of view of fire safety.

label: Fire on the Moon (FM2 concept)
text: NASA Glenn proposed a small chamber to conduct the first-ever combustion tests on another world.
quote: We propose to use a small chamber to conduct the first-ever combustion tests on another world.

label: Official knowledge gap (2021)
text: A 2021 NASA exploration-atmospheres decision memo names material flammability in low and partial gravity a significant knowledge gap.
quote: Identifies material flammability in low- and partial-gravity at these conditions to be a significant knowledge gap for exploration

label: NRC decadal survey
text: The 2011 NRC decadal survey made fire-safety research on flammability screening and suppression one of its highest-priority enabling recommendations.
quote: One of the highest-priority enabling recommendations made in Chapter 9: Applied Physical Sciences in Space was “Fire safety research to improve methods for screening materials for flammability and fire suppression in space environments.

label: Lunar buoyant flow
text: Scaling: a small burning sample with about 100 cm/s buoyant flow on Earth would have about 40 cm/s on the Moon.
quote: if a small (1-cm), engulfed, burning sample on Earth has U1 ≈100 cm/s, then on the Moon the same sample would have U1 ≈40 cm/s

label: Artemis 3 cabin atmosphere
text: Large-scale fire-growth tests were run to inform the choice of cabin atmosphere for the Artemis 3 mission.
quote: Large-scale fire growth tests were performed to inform the decision regarding cabin atmosphere for the Artemis 3 mission

label: Conservatism varies
text: How conservative Test 1 is varies with material and cannot be determined from the test data.
quote: The degree of conservatism varies with material and cannot be determined from the test data

label: Depends on flow
text: Whether Test 1 is conservative may depend on the flow velocity and direction chosen for the comparison.
quote: The question of conservatism of Test 1 therefore may rest on the determination of velocity and flow direction at which to compare

label: Thin high-O2 database
text: Test 1 is run at the atmosphere of use, but its database is smaller at higher oxygen concentrations.
quote: Test 1 is run at atmosphere of use, though data base is smaller at higher oxygen concentrations.

label: Skylab and Apollo atmospheres
text: Exploration cabins may use enriched-oxygen, low-pressure atmospheres, as Skylab (70% oxygen, 5 psia) and Apollo (100% oxygen, 5 psia) did.
quote: Exploration environments may have an enriched oxygen, low pressure atmosphere. • Skylab 70% oxygen, 5 psia • Apollo 100 % oxygen, 5 psia

label: Smoldering not tested
text: Smoldering combustion is not covered by NASA-STD-6001 Test 1.
quote: Smoldering not covered under NASA Std. 6001, Test 1.

label: Most stringent at 1 g
text: Test 1 is an upward flammability test, considered the most stringent test in normal gravity.
quote: NASA STD 6001, Test 1 is an upward flammability test, considered the most stringent test in normal gravity.

label: Artemis exploration atmosphere
text: NASA Artemis requirements for sustained missions target an average cabin pressure of 8.2 psi (56.5 kPa) with 34% oxygen.
quote: NASA Artemis requirements for sustained missions are targeting an average pressure of 8.2 psi (56.5 kPa) and a 34% oxygen concentration as one solution to those trade-offs.

label: Above 30% O2 is less known
text: Less is known about material flammability above 30% oxygen, so NASA teams have also tested a vehicle atmosphere kept below 30%.
quote: less is known about oxygen concentrations above 30% oxygen, leading to flammability concerns such that NASA teams have alternatively performed testing utilizing a vehicle atmopshere that stays below 30%

label: Blowoff needs strong flow
text: A flame blows out when airflow is too fast for reactants to react while hot; Earth's stronger buoyant flows make this easier than on the Moon.
quote: A flame can extinguish if the cabin airflow is high enough that the reactants don’t have time to react while the mixture is hot enough.

label: Lunar smouldering
text: Unlike in still microgravity air, natural convection in lunar gravity might supply enough oxygen for a smouldering fire to propagate.
quote: A smouldering flame in lunar gravity, however, might have sufficient natural airflow to promote the additional oxygen concentration needed to propagate

label: ISS spacesuit pressure
text: The Shuttle/ISS Extravehicular Mobility Unit spacesuit maintains 4.3 psi (29.6 kPa).
quote: Extravehicular Mobility Unit used during the Space Shuttle program and aboard the International Space Station (referred to as “Station Suit” throughout this paper) maintains a pressure of 4.3 psi (29.6 kPa)

label: Spacesuits run on pure O2
text: Both ISS-era spacesuits, the US EMU and the Russian Orlan, operate with a 100% oxygen atmosphere.
quote: Both systems operate with a 100% oxygen atmosphere

label: Apollo 1 (1967)
text: The Apollo 1 fire was made worse by materials becoming more flammable in the command module's high-pressure, pure-oxygen atmosphere.
quote: the Apollo 1 fire was exacerbated by the increased flammability of materials inside the command module under its high-pressure, pure-oxygen atmosphere

label: ISS cabin atmosphere
text: Since Skylab, the Space Shuttle and ISS have operated at sea-level conditions: air with 21% oxygen at 14.7 psia.
quote: the Space Shuttle and the International Space Station (ISS) have operated at normal sea-level conditions (air, 21% oxygen/79% nitrogen by volume at 14.7 psia total pressure)

label: Orion and Altair design atmospheres
text: Constellation-era designs: Orion and the Altair lunar lander were to operate between 8.0 and 14.9 psia with up to 30% and 34% oxygen respectively.
quote: The Crew Exploration Vehicle (CEV), Orion, and the lunar lander, Altair, are designed to operate from 8.0 to 14.9 psia and at a maximum of 30 and 34% oxygen concentration respectively.

label: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
text: NASA screens materials with NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, an upward burning test at the worst-case atmosphere in which the material will be used.
quote: NASA tests materials for flammability using NASA STD-6001 Test 1 (ref. 3), which is an upward burning test at the worst-case atmospheric conditions in which the material will be used.

label: 1-g limits not conservative
text: Drop-tower comparisons found 1-g Test 1 flammability limits generally not conservative for the thin spacecraft materials tested.
quote: As shown in figure 5, the 1g flammability limits are generally not conservative for these materials

label: Why low g can be worse
text: Without buoyancy, convective heat loss is greatly reduced, so materials can burn at lower oxygen in low gravity than in 1 g with concurrent flow.
quote: For concurrent (upward) flow conditions, it is reasonable for materials to be flammable at lower oxygen concentration in low-g than in 1-g because in the absence of buoyancy, the heat loss due to convective flow is greatly reduced.

label: Max spacecraft ventilation
text: About 30 cm/s is a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity for flammability comparisons.
quote: compared with 0g values obtained at a concurrent flow of 30 cm/s, which is a reasonable maximum local spacecraft ventilation velocity

label: Nominal ventilation range
text: Nominal spacecraft ventilation flows span about 5 to 20 cm/s.
quote: It is seen that over virtually the entire range of spacecraft atmospheres and flow conditions (5 to 20 cm/s nominal range (ref. 11)

label: Space exploration atmosphere
text: The proposed exploration cabin atmosphere uses 52.7 to 58.6 kPa total pressure with 30 to 34% oxygen, chosen with material flammability in mind.
quote: The proposed environment uses a total cabin pressure of 52.7 to 58.6 kPa with an oxygen concentration of 30 to 34% by volume and was chosen with material flammability in mind.

label: Earth tests can't mimic cabin flow
text: Spacecraft ventilation flows of about 10–20 cm/s cannot easily be reproduced on Earth, where buoyant flow of about 40 cm/s dominates.
quote: This low velocity flows encountered in a spacecraft are on the order of ~10–20 cm/s and cannot be easily replicated on earth because the buoyant flow (~40 cm/s) dominates over the forced flow

label: Test 1 is pass/fail
text: Test 1 is a pass-fail upward flame spread test, valid only at the specific atmosphere tested.
quote: It is pass-fail and is only valid at the atmosphere tested.

label: Cabin leak leaves pure O2
text: In an Orion cabin-leak scenario, the depressurizing cabin would end up holding only oxygen, at near-vacuum pressure, leaked from the crew's suits.
quote: Ultimately, the only gas in the CM cabin would be oxygen at near vacuum pressures from suit leakage.

label: Why the boundary is U-shaped
text: The flammability minimum sits at a flow strong enough to sustain heat release but weak enough not to sweep fuel out of the flame zone before reacting.
quote: This minimum occurs where the flow still permits enough heat release to sustain the flame but not so strong that it sweeps the fuel out of the hot flame zone before it can react.

label: Decadal Survey
text: The Decadal Survey, quoted by the BASS-II team, states that present normal-gravity materials tests are not adequate for reduced-gravity scenarios.
quote: Present tests, performed in normal gravity, are not adequate for reduced gravity scenarios.

label: A 1-g test that predicts 0 g
text: Marcum, Olson and Ferkul propose a normal-gravity rod blowoff test that extrapolates to zero stretch to estimate microgravity flammability limits, which current methods cannot resolve.
quote: We describe a new normal gravity ‘upward flame spread test’ method which extrapolates the linear blowoff boundary to the zero stretch limit in order to resolve microgravity flammability limits—something current methods cannot do.

label: Worst case on Earth, not in space
text: NASA's upward burning test in normal gravity is considered the worst-case geometry on Earth, but it may not be conservative for flammability in space.
quote: using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space.

label: BASS-II outlined the U
text: Crew-adapted flow changes during BASS-II, including blowoff extinctions, gave flight data outlining the U-shaped flammability boundary.
quote: blowoff extinctions, that proved to be very valuable data in outlining the U-shaped flammability boundary

label: Saffire IV-V on Test 1
text: Saffire found NASA's 1-g Test 1 is good at flagging highly flammable materials but cannot show a material won't burn in low gravity.
quote: The test is quite successful at identifying highly flammable materials; however, the test cannot be assumed to indicate that a material will not burn under those conditions in low gravity.

label: Ignition vs airflow
text: In low gravity, still air likely makes materials less ignitable than a gentle flow; the most ignitable condition is likely at low flow rates.
quote: For ignition, however, quiescent conditions will likely make the sample less ignitable than with convection present. The most ignitable condition is likely to be at low flow rates

label: Saffire I-III
text: Saffire's large-scale orbital tests showed spacecraft fires can grow to significant size and persist long enough to concern crew and vehicle.
quote: These tests demonstrated that spacecraft fires could grow to significant size and persist long enough to be of concern to the crew and the spacecraft.

label: Saffire on Cygnus
text: Saffire studied large-sample flame spread and its effect on the whole pressurized spacecraft inside Cygnus, in orbit after it left the ISS.
quote: The spread and growth of flames over large solid fuel samples and their effect on the pressurized spacecraft were studied inside the Cygnus spacecraft while in orbit after departing the International Space Station.

label: Saffire IV-V
text: Saffire showed that at increased oxygen, thin charring fuels cannot be assumed to extinguish rapidly in still air.
quote: Extinguishment of thin charring fuels at increased oxygen cannot be assumed to occur rapidly in quiescent conditions.

label: Why Saffire
text: Without large-scale low-gravity fire data, spacecraft designers have based designs and safety precautions on 1-g understanding of spread, extinction, detection and suppression.
quote: The lack of this experimental data has forced spacecraft designers to base their designs and safety precautions on 1-g understanding of flame spread, flame self-extinguishment, fire detection, and suppression.

label: Saffire VI conclusion
text: Saffire's authors say further work is needed to extend their spacecraft fire results to the partial gravity expected on the Moon and Mars.
quote: Further work will be needed to extend these results to the partial gravity environment expected on future mission to the moon and Mars.

label: Saffire IV-VI scale
text: Saffire tested practical-scale fires of 1.5 to 3.2 kW inside unmanned spacecraft with 17 to 19 cubic meters of free air.
quote: Practical scale fires ranging from 1.5 to 3.2 kW were tested in unmanned spacecraft with free air volumes of 17 to 19 cubic meters.

label: Saffire VI atmosphere control
text: For Saffire VI, operators vented Cygnus to a requested pressure and the experiment released oxygen to reach each test's target atmosphere.
quote: The Northrup Grumman operators vented the spacecraft to the requested pressure and the Saffire experiment then released oxygen to bring the spacecraft to the desired condition (Table 1).

label: Saffire-II objective
text: Saffire-II set out to test whether flammability limits measured in 1-g with NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 match those in low gravity.
quote: One main objective of the Saffire-II experiment is to ascertain if the flammability limits determined in 1-g using NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 are the same as those in low-gravity.

label: Saffire IV-V
text: Saffire IV and V gave the first measurements of combustion products from large-scale fires in microgravity.
quote: Saffire-IV and V provided the first measurements of combustion products from large-scale fires in microgravity

label: Saffire approach
text: Saffire offered the opportunity to study large-scale fires in microgravity with lower risk to the crew.
quote: Opportunity to study large-scale fires in microgravity with lower risk to crew

label: FLEX data volume
text: FLEX produced a wealth of droplet combustion data across many fuels, fuel mixtures and ambient conditions, from over 1500 tests.
quote: A wealth of experimental data with a variety of fuels, fuel mixtures, and ambient conditions (over 1500 tests)

label: Suppression data gap
text: Without reduced-gravity suppression data, suppressant choices for lunar and Martian missions will rest on the same studies and normal-gravity data used for the ISS.
quote: The selection of fire suppressants and suppression strategies for NASA’s Lunar and Martian exploration missions will be based on the same studies and normal-gravity data unless reduced gravity fire suppression data is obtained.

label: Partial-g suppression data
text: CO2 fire-suppression data were obtained at 0.1 g, 0.17 g (lunar), 0.38 g (Martian) and 0.5 g.
quote: Data obtained for CO2 at 0.1-go, 0.17-go(Lunar), 0.38-go (Martian), and 0.5-go

label: ISS fire response
text: On the ISS, fire response procedure stops ventilation flow and removes power once a fire alarm is annunciated.
quote: Fire response procedure on ISS dictates that ventilation flow is ceased and power removed after annunciation of a fire alarm

label: SoFIE flammability team
text: NASA's SoFIE flammability team states a flame can be sustained at lower oxygen in reduced gravity, including 0 g, lunar and Martian gravity.
quote: In reduced gravity (0g, Lunar g, Martian g), a flame can be sustained at lower O2.

label: 1-g screening
text: In NASA's 1-g flammability screening tests, flames extinguish by blowoff, according to SoFIE's flammability researchers.
quote: In the 1-g screening tests, flames extinguish by blowoff.

label: Quenching and blowoff
text: In SoFIE's thin-PMMA flame images, flames quench radiatively below 2 cm/s airflow and near blowoff extinction above 40 cm/s.
quote: radiative quenching when flow velocity goes below 2 cm/s. Right: Flame nearing blow off extinction as the flow velocity crosses 40 cm/s.

label: Exploration atmosphere
text: SoFIE researchers note that even in 1-g, few thin-sheet materials are rated at the 34% O2, 8.2 psia exploration atmosphere.
quote: Thin fuel sheets: few materials rated even in 1g at 34% O2, 8.2 psia (exploration atmosphere).

label: SoFIE goal
text: SoFIE aims to make cabin material selection safer and to validate NASA's 1-g flammability test protocols for low-gravity fires.
quote: Safer selection of cabin materials and validate NASA materials flammability selection 1-g test protocols for low-gravity fires

label: Detectors built on 1-g data
text: As of 2007, all spacecraft smoke detectors had been designed from normal-gravity data because microgravity smoke data were lacking.
quote: Owing to the absence of microgravity smoke data, all current spacecraft smoke detectors were designed based upon normal-g conditions.

label: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
text: BASS-II's PSI record notes NASA's normal-gravity upward-burning screening test is considered worst case on Earth but may not be conservative for flammability in space.
quote: using an upward burning test in normal gravity, which is considered to be the worst-case geometry for flammability of the material on Earth. However, it may not be conservative for flammability in space.

label: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
text: BASS's PSI record states NASA spacecraft materials selection uses NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, which sorts materials by 1-g behavior without considering low-gravity effects.
quote: Current NASA spacecraft materials selection is based on a standard test method (NASA–STD–6001 Test 1) that segregates material based on 1-g behavior without consideration of low gravity effects.

label: ACME BRE test atmospheres
text: ACME BRE planned microgravity tests at NASA-considered crew atmospheres: 14.7 psia with 21% O2, 10.2 psia with 26.5%, and 8.2 psia with 34%.
quote: NASA - considered atmosphere for human space missions will be examined: 14.7 psia, 21 % oxygen: 10.2 psia, 26.5 %; and 8.2 psia, 34 % oxygen.

label: BRE: elevated O2, no airflow
text: In BRE, flames kept burning without airflow in elevated-oxygen atmospheres considered for future spacecraft, while flames at 21% oxygen self-extinguished quickly.
quote: The ongoing combustion without air flow was notably seen in elevated-oxygen atmospheres which are being considered for use in future spacecraft, whereas such flames in a normal atmosphere of 21% oxygen self-extinguished in a short time.

label: E-FIELD Flames
text: In E-FIELD Flames, the applied electric field acted on ions from chemi-ionization, driving ion-driven convection that influenced flame behavior.
quote: The electric field interacts with ions generated through chemi-ionization during combustion, driving ion-driving convection and influencing flame behavior.

label: E-FIELD Flames: stated purpose
text: E-FIELD Flames' PSI record says the research was not conducted to serve space applications, though findings might aid future space combustion devices.
quote: The E-FIELD Flames research is not being conducted to serve any space applications, but it is possible that its findings could aid the development of future space-based combustion devices

label: FLEX-2 test atmospheres
text: FLEX-2's ISS droplet tests varied pressure from 0.5 to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration from 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction.
quote: The chamber was filled with the appropriate atmosphere, which was varied in pressure between 0.5 atm to 3.0 atm and O2 concentration between 0.1 to 0.4 mole fraction with the diluent gas making up the balance.

label: Saffire: data gap
text: Saffire's PSI record states spacecraft designers lack microgravity fire data on which to base fire safety designs and procedures.
quote: There is a significant lack of microgravity data available for spacecraft designers on which to base their fire safety designs and procedures.

label: NASA-STD-6001 Test 1
text: Test 1 fails a material that burns more than 12 inches from a standard igniter.
quote: Its simple pass-fail criteria eliminates materials that burn for more than 12 inches from a standardized ignition source.

label: Screened at 1 g
text: Test 1 runs in Earth gravity and assumes a material that passes is safe for spaceflight.
quote: The test is conducted in normal Earth gravity, with the assumption that if a material passes the 1-g test, then it is considered safe for spaceflight.

label: Olson 2004
text: Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires; its adequacy at lunar or Martian gravity is unknown.
quote: There is compelling evidence that the Test 1 may not be the worst case for spacecraft fires, and we don't have enough information to assess if it is adequate at Lunar or Martian gravity levels.

label: Passes at 1 g, burns elsewhere
text: Some materials that won't burn in 1 g will burn in 0 g with low flow, or at lunar gravity.
quote: Theoretical and experimental results have demonstrated that some materials that will not burn in 1-g will burn in 0-g (with a low-speed flow) or in partial gravity (such as Lunar-g).

label: Minimum near lunar g
text: The oxygen needed for flammability reaches a minimum near lunar gravity.
quote: Related work suggests that oxygen concentration for flammability reaches a minimum value in the vicinity of g = g Lunar.

label: Blowoff branch (high flow)
text: With strong buoyant flow, air can enter a flame faster than its chemistry can keep pace.
quote: The speed of the air entering the flame can be so high, however, that the chemical reactions are unable to keep pace.

label: Quenching branch (low flow)
text: With too little flow, a flame starves of fresh oxygen and cannot survive indefinitely.
quote: As demonstrated by the data above, the flame cannot survive indefinitely without a supply of fresh oxygen.

label: Why the Moon can be worse
text: At lunar gravity buoyant oxygen supply persists but slows, so a material marginal on Earth may burn.
quote: The same material may be flammable at a lower gravity level (for example, on the Moon) since the crucial mechanism of buoyant oxygen entrainment at the flame base is still present, but at a slower rate

label: Nearly the most flammable
text: Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition, per numerical and experimental evidence.
quote: Numerical and experimental evidence suggests that Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

label: Habitat fires at partial g
text: Partial-g habitat fires are expected to be substantially worse than at 0 g and possibly worse than at 1 g.
quote: Consequently, partial-g fire in an extraterrestrial habitat is a real hazard that is expected to be substantially worse than in 0-g and potentially worse than even 1-g.

label: FM2
text: FM2 will burn four solid fuel samples in real, long-duration lunar gravity.
quote: Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) will burn a total of four solid fuel samples in quiescent habitable atmospheres in actual long duration Lunar gravity (Fig. 1).

label: FM2 launch
text: The first combustion experiments on another world are planned to launch in late 2026.
quote: The first-ever combustion experiments on another world will be performed, with a planned launch date of late 2026.

label: FM2 goal
text: FM2 results will bridge NASA's 1-g screening test and real behaviour in reduced gravity.
quote: The results will provide a bridge between the current 1-g material screening method and actual behavior in reduced gravity.

label: Drop towers & aircraft
text: Drop towers (5 s) and aircraft (~25 s) give too little time for significant flame development.
quote: Partial gravity tests can be performed in drop towers [8] and aboard aircraft [2], but the available times are too short to provide significant flame development (5 s for drop tower and ~25 s for aircraft).

label: Rotating sounding rocket
text: A spinning sounding rocket simulated lunar gravity for about 150 s, with Coriolis uncertainty.
quote: A sounding rocket utilizing vehicle rotation to simulate Lunar gravity provided test times on the order of 150 s, burning two different materials, but again the Coriolis force introduces uncertainty.

label: Exploration Atmosphere
text: The lunar-habitat Exploration Atmosphere was revised to 8.2 psia and 34% O2.
quote: Current plans for M2M habitats on the Lunar surface require EVA, thus EA recommendation became 8 psia and 32% O2 but was revised to 8.2 psia and 34% O2 to decrease hypoxia exposure.

label: The trade-off
text: The Exploration Atmosphere eases EVAs but makes fire management harder in higher-than-normal O2.
quote: Unfortunately, the benefits of EA in support of safe and efficient EVAs comes with the challenge of fire management in a higher-than-normal O2% environment.

label: NESC assessment
text: Raising O2 concentration at low cabin pressure increases material flammability.
quote: A consequence of raising O2 concentration to sustain O2 partial pressure in a low-pressure environment is that the flammability of materials increases with increasing O2 concentration.

label: HEO-DM-1006
text: Exploration missions with frequent EVA need 8.2 psia cabins with at least 33.7% O2.
quote: HEO-DM-1006 [ref. 15] specifies that a nominal total cabin pressure of 8.2 psia and O2 greater than or equal to 33.7% is needed for Exploration missions with high-frequency EVA.

label: Lander, habitat, rover
text: The lander, lunar habitat and pressurized rover will nominally run 8.2 psia and 34% O2.
quote: HLS, Lunar habitat and pressurized rover will nominally use 8.2 psia / 34% O2, 66% N2

label: Moon base atmosphere
text: Moon base and rover atmospheres will likely be at least 30% O2 at 10.2 psi or less.
quote: The intermediate oxygen concentration used on the Moon will likely be 30% or greater, with a corresponding pressure of 10.2 psi or less.

label: +40% oxygen
text: That is over 40% more oxygen than Earth's air, making materials much more flammable.
quote: Compared to Earth's atmosphere, that's more than a 40% increase in the oxygen concentration making materials much more flammable.

label: Data gap above 30% O2
text: NASA has limited material flammability data above 30% O2.
quote: However, NASA has limited material flammability data at O2 concentration higher than 30% (F-12a).

label: Max O2 36-40%
text: With control bands and sensor accuracy, habitat O2 could peak at 36-40%.
quote: When provision is made for O2 concentration control bands and sensor accuracy, the maximum O2 concentration could be between 36 and 40%, but the exact numbers will depend on specific vehicle design and hardware capability.

label: Control band
text: Cabin O2 control bands are expected to allow up to 37%.
quote: Control bands are expected to allow up to 37% O2

label: 37% O2 certification
text: Textiles are being certified for 34% O2 plus a 3% margin: a 37% O2 target.
quote: Now, the agency focus is on certifying textiles for use in 34% O2 plus a 3% margin, resulting in a target of 37% O2.

label: CFI-G
text: ACME's CFI-G ran the highest-oxygen microgravity tests in PSI.
quote: Microgravity tests with the highest oxygen concentrations were conducted as part of the ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G).

label: Up to 85% O2
text: CFI-G flowed up to 85% oxygen from a spherical burner, making an inside-out flame.
quote: an oxygen-nitrogen mixture of up to 85% oxygen flowed from the spherical burner creating an inside-out flame.

label: Challenge brief
text: PSI currently holds no partial-gravity combustion data.
quote: there is currently no partial-gravity combustion data available in PSI.

label: LUCI & FM2
text: Partial-gravity data are expected from LUCI and FM2.
quote: We expect such data will be added in the future, for example from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment.

label: E-FIELD mimicry
text: ACME's E-FIELD Flames mimicked partial gravity by acting on flame ions with an electric field.
quote: Partial gravity was mimicked in ACME's Electric-Field Effects on Laminar Diffusion Flames (E-FIELD Flames) experiment through the effect of the electric field on the ions that naturally occur in flames.

label: The naive bound
text: The brief suggests 0-g and 1-g results could bound behaviour at intermediate gravity.
quote: Microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound what occurs at intermediate gravity levels.

label: Detection in PSI
text: Fire detection was tested in microgravity by SAME and SAME-R.
quote: Fire detection was tested in microgravity through the Smoke and Aerosol Measurement Experiment studies (SAME and SAME-R).

label: Apollo 1 (1967)
text: In Apollo 1's pure-oxygen cabin the fire spread quickly and ruptured the Command Module pressure vessel.
quote: Because of the pure oxygen atmosphere, the fire spread quickly, causing a rapid rise in temperature and pressure that led to the rupture of the Command Module pressure vessel.

label: Apollo 13 (1970)
text: An oxygen tank blew up in flight, and the second oxygen tank then failed.
quote: oxygen tank number two blew up, leading to the subsequent failure of tank number one.

label: Mir (1997)
text: A fire in an oxygen-generating system endangered all six crew aboard Mir.
quote: On Feb. 24, 1997, the six crew members aboard the Russian space station Mir faced significant danger when a fire ignited in an oxygen generating system.
